questions.q: How many major seasonal releases does Salesforce ship per year, and what is each one's typical effect on the API version number?
options: One release per year, with no version change
Three releases per year (Spring, Summer, Winter), each typically introducing a new API version number
Twelve releases per year, one per month
Releases happen on no fixed schedule at all
questions.explain: Salesforce's Spring, Summer, and Winter releases happen three times a year, and each typically increments the API version number by about 1.

questions.q: What API version does this lesson verify corresponds to Spring '26?
questions.explain: This lesson verified against Salesforce's own documentation that Spring '26 corresponds to API version 66.0.

questions.q: What does pinning a specific API version in every call protect an integration from?
options: Running out of data storage
Behavior silently changing underneath the integration as the org's underlying platform gets upgraded through new seasonal releases
Having to authenticate with OAuth
Needing to use JSON instead of XML
questions.explain: Salesforce supports old API versions for a long deprecation window specifically so a pinned integration keeps behaving the same way even as the org itself upgrades.

questions.q: How can a client discover which API versions an org currently supports?
options: GET /services/data/v61.0/limits
GET /services/data/ (the unversioned root resource)
POST /services/oauth2/token
GET /services/data/v61.0/sobjects/
questions.explain: The unversioned root resource GET /services/data/ returns the full list of API versions the org supports, each with a label and URL.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should an integration move to a newer API version?
options: Automatically and immediately on every seasonal release, with no testing
Never — once pinned, a version should never be changed
Deliberately, when a specific newer capability is actually needed, after testing — not reflexively on every release
Only when the old version is deleted entirely, with no warning
questions.explain: The practical approach is staying on a stable pinned version by default and moving deliberately, after testing, when a specific new capability is actually needed.
